title: fastapi-full-stack-template: authentication and authorization from login form to protected route
intro: You will follow one login through fastapi-full-stack-template: the React form in frontend/src/routes/login.tsx, the OAuth2 password endpoint, the JWT, the Authorization header, and the FastAPI dependencies that guard routes. Afterwards you can trace a request through both halves, explain who may see what, and add a protected route correctly.
subject: Authentication and authorization, end to end: from the login form to a protected API route
docsNote: The READMEs only list "JWT authentication" and "secure password hashing"; no page describes the token flow, the localStorage choice, or the superuser/owner rules. A short auth section in backend/README.md would help.

chapters.title: Credentials in: the login endpoint and password hashing
chapters.goal: Explain how POST /login/access-token in backend/app/api/routes/login.py verifies credentials via crud.authenticate, hashes with pwdlib (Argon2 plus legacy Bcrypt) and issues an HS256 JWT from security.create_access_token.
chapters.hootIntro: Every session in this template starts at one endpoint, POST /login/access-token, so let's follow a password from the form post to a signed JWT.

steps.title: Four files, one login
steps.body: The backend lives in `backend/app`. The login route is `api/routes/login.py`; it delegates the password check to `crud.authenticate` in `crud.py`, which uses the hashing helpers in `core/security.py`. The signing key and token lifetime come from `Settings` in `core/config.py`. The route itself stays thin: it only turns a result into an HTTP answer.

sources.why: The endpoint that ties the other files together

stops.annotation: `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` reads form fields `username` and `password`. In this project `username` carries the email. A bad login or an inactive user gives a 400; otherwise a `Token` is returned.
`authenticate` looks the user up by email, verifies the password, and returns the `User` or `None`. If the hasher says the stored hash is outdated, it saves the new one.

`password_hash` is a pwdlib `PasswordHash` with Argon2 first and Bcrypt second. `verify_password` calls `verify_and_update`, returning `(ok, new_hash_or_None)`. `create_access_token` signs `exp` and `sub` with `SECRET_KEY` using HS256.
`SECRET_KEY` has no default, so it must come from the environment. `ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES` defaults to 8 days, which login.py turns into a `timedelta`.

steps.title: Same work for unknown emails
steps.prompt: Click the line that runs a password verification even though no user was found.
steps.explanation: Line 50 verifies the submitted password against `DUMMY_HASH` when the email is unknown. Response time then looks the same whether or not the account exists, which the comment calls timing attack prevention.

steps.title: What the token carries: a signed JWT
steps.concept: A JWT is a signed, base64-encoded set of claims. With HS256 the same secret signs and verifies it, so anyone holding the secret can mint valid tokens, and nobody else can alter one undetected.
steps.applied: `create_access_token` in `security.py` puts two claims in the token: `exp` (now plus `expires_delta`) and `sub` (the user id as a string). It signs them with `settings.SECRET_KEY` and `ALGORITHM = "HS256"`. The server stores no session: the token is the session, and later requests are checked by decoding it.

sources.why: Subject is user.id and lifetime comes from settings

steps.title: Hashing: Argon2 now, Bcrypt tolerated
steps.body: `PasswordHash((Argon2Hasher(), BcryptHasher()))` makes Argon2 the hasher for new passwords and keeps Bcrypt only to verify old ones. When someone with a Bcrypt hash logs in, `verify_and_update` returns a fresh Argon2 hash and `authenticate` writes it back. So legacy users migrate silently, with no reset campaign. Settings also refuse the `changethis` placeholder for `SECRET_KEY` outside development.

steps.question: A user whose stored hash starts with `$2` (Bcrypt) logs in with the right password. What does the test suite expect afterwards?
choices: The stored hash now starts with `$argon2` and the login still returns 200
The login fails with 400 until the user resets the password
The stored hash stays Bcrypt, since only new users get Argon2
The user is marked inactive until an admin approves the change
steps.hint: Read the two tests near the end of test_login.py that compare `user.hashed_password` before and after.
steps.explanation: `test_login_with_bcrypt_password_upgrades_to_argon2` asserts a 200, then that the hash starts with `$argon2` and that verifying again needs no further update. The Argon2 counterpart test asserts the hash is unchanged.

steps.title: Order of a successful login
steps.prompt: Put the server-side steps of POST /login/access-token in order.
items: `verify_password` checks the hash and may return an upgraded one
steps.explanation: The route receives the form, authenticate verifies (and may rehash), the route checks `is_active`, then the JWT is signed and wrapped in `Token`. The activity check lives in the route, not in `authenticate`.

takeaways: POST /login/access-token in login.py takes form fields, delegates to crud.authenticate, and returns a Token with a JWT signed with SECRET_KEY (HS256, sub and exp).
crud.authenticate runs verify_password against DUMMY_HASH for unknown emails, so timing does not reveal which accounts exist.
security.py hashes with Argon2 and still verifies Bcrypt, upgrading old hashes on successful login.

chapters.title: Guarding routes: OAuth2PasswordBearer and the deps chain
chapters.goal: Trace how backend/app/api/deps.py turns a Bearer token into a User through reusable_oauth2, get_current_user and the CurrentUser alias, and name the status codes each failure produces (403, 404, 400).

chapters.title: Authorization: superusers, ownership and the Items rules
chapters.goal: Distinguish authentication from the two authorization patterns used here: get_current_active_superuser as a route dependency (users.py, utils.py) and the is_superuser/owner_id checks inside backend/app/api/routes/items.py.

chapters.title: The browser side: form, token storage and route guards
chapters.goal: Follow the React flow: the zod-validated form in frontend/src/routes/login.tsx, useAuth.login storing access_token in localStorage, client.setConfig in main.tsx attaching it, and beforeLoad guards in _layout.tsx and admin.tsx plus the 401/403 logout handler.

chapters.title: Proving it: token reset flow and the tests that exercise auth
chapters.goal: Explain how the password-reset JWT (generate_password_reset_token in utils.py, /reset-password/) reuses the SECRET_KEY, and how pytest (user_authentication_headers) and Playwright (auth.setup.ts storageState) log in to test protected routes.
